title: What Flock Actually Costs Cities Across the Country
gist: WIRED's review of public records from about two dozen Flock Safety customers shows city spending climbing several-fold within a few years (e.g. Alpharetta to $381,000, Savannah from $33,000 to $193,500), driven by a land-and-expand model of HOA entry, multiyear price locks and product bundling. A few customers are cancelling over price rises and low utility.

insights.claim: Flock started by selling license plate readers to homeowner associations in 2017 and began selling to police in 2019, so police could start by tapping HOA cameras already in place instead of building a network from scratch.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Private-camera footprints give Flock a built-in wedge into municipal contracts, and incompatibility with other vendors deepens lock-in.
insights.locator: How Flock Gets in the Door

insights.claim: Individual city bills ballooned: Covington went from $40,000 in 2020 to $159,000 in 2025 and $201,000 through August 2026; Alpharetta's annual bill reached $381,000 by 2025; Savannah went from $33,000 (2020) to $193,500 (2025); Snellville from $5,000 (2021) to $163,275 (2025).
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Multi-year expansion per customer implies strong net revenue retention for Flock as pilots become large recurring budget lines.
insights.locator: In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington

insights.claim: Flock uses discounts for multiyear commitments: Alpharetta's 2024 five-year deal was $232,500 cheaper than five one-year agreements, and a customer manager pitched a five-year price lock after new Falcon cameras rose from $2,500 to $3,000.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Price-lock framing converts rising list prices into long contracts, boosting backlog visibility and switching costs, and leaving taxpayers committed for years.
insights.quote: If you would like to lock in your current camera rates, Flock is offering a 5-year contract

insights.claim: Bundling consolidates vendors: Greenfield, California replaced five contracts with three companies by a five-year Flock deal at $136,940 a year (about $24,000 more than before) that added cameras, Flock911 and drones from Aerodrome, which Flock acquired in 2024.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Platform bundling and acquisitions let Flock displace point-solution vendors while raising spend per customer.

insights.claim: Police-tech vendors use discounts and free trials to get in, such as a 90-day trial of the Nova product in Alpharetta, and an EFF analyst says that once police try a tool it becomes hard to remove it.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Free-trial-to-contract funnels and political stickiness imply low churn for surveillance vendors.

insights.claim: Flock sorts agencies into 14 software pricing buckets by size (Bucket 1 from about $2,000 to $115,500; Bucket 14 custom), with hardware at flat annual rates: cameras and readers $3,000 to $5,200 a year plus $150 to $2,750 install, gunshot detectors $8,500 to $35,000, drones $50,000 to $150,000, and mobile trailers $20,000 to $25,000.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Subscription hardware pricing makes revenue recurring, with drones the highest ticket per unit.

insights.claim: Flock keeps ownership of equipment, so cities pay for damaged or stolen units and must return gear if they leave; flat replacement rates are $800 per camera, $500 per pole and $1,300 for both, up from $500 and $150 in 2021.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Vandalism creates incremental replacement revenue for Flock and shifts cost to municipalities.
insights.locator: Flock also has a pricing plan for replacing

insights.claim: Flock's pricing looks comparable to rivals: Axon quoted Denver $150,000 to install and maintain 50 cameras for a year, and Motorola charged Manti, Utah $4,704 for one plate reader; Motorola also signed a $54 million Louisiana policing technology agreement.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Competitors price similarly, so differentiation rests on integration and bundling, not price.
insights.locator: Though prices vary depending on the size

insights.claim: Some cities overstated vandalism costs: Winona and Rutherfordton claimed $3,000 and $3,500 per camera versus the listed $800, and Derby, Kansas claimed $26,000 for 10 cameras versus an estimated $8,000 to $13,000.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Official cost figures in the backlash against Flock can be inflated, so check against contract rates.
insights.locator: Some cities have gone out of their way

insights.claim: Flock is cheap relative to helicopters or hiring officers but can top other technology line items: Pasadena, Texas budgeted $427,133 for Flock versus $500,842 for body camera software and $500,000 for Motorola maintenance.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Flock is now a top tech budget item in some departments, making it a visible target in budget fights.

insights.claim: Some customers are leaving: Lorain County, Ohio is cancelling after Flock planned a 17 percent two-year rate rise for 15 cameras, and Killingworth, Connecticut ended its contract over privacy concerns and little utility for its trooper after paying $14,600 for four cameras.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Price escalation after expansion and privacy backlash are the early churn drivers to monitor.
insights.locator: Why Some Customers Are Ditching Flock
